strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in federated learning: handling heterogeneous data where knowledge is shared across multiple levels of granularity (globally shared, subgroup/cluster shared, and client-specific).

The progressive training and residual-learning mechanism (training and freezing earlier levels, then learning residuals at finer levels) provides an intuitive and communication-efficient way to optimize multi-level models without exchanging all level parameters in every round.
Extensive empirical evaluations are conducted across CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet under various non-IID partitions, showing consistent accuracy improvements over the selected baselines.

Because the learning rate must be strictly positive, no valid learning rate can satisfy this condition near convergence, invalidating the convergence claim. Similarly, in Theorem 1 (Appendix D.3), the required step size is bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\sum \|	heta_i - \Theta\|^2})$, which collapses to zero as local models approach cluster centroids.

Uncontrolled model capacity and inference/storage overhead: FeMAM constructs an additive ensemble of up to $L=5$ ResNet-9 models per client. Consequently, clients incur up to $5\times$ the memory footprint, model parameter storage, and inference FLOPs. In contrast, all evaluated baselines (FedAvg, Ditto, FeSEM, pFedMe, etc.) are restricted to a single ResNet-9 model. Without baselines with matched parameter counts (e.g., deeper/wider models or an additive ensemble of 5 FedAvg/Ditto models), it is impossible to disentangle whether the gains stem from the multi-level hierarchy or simply increased model capacity.

Limited conceptual novelty over prior additive and clustered FL: Additive modeling combining global, cluster, and personalized components has already been proposed in prior work (e.g., Ma et al., NeurIPS 2023 [34]; Agarwal et al., 2020 [18]). Extending this from 2–3 levels to $L$ levels sequentially with standard $K$-means and greedy validation pruning is a relatively incremental extension.

Presentation flaws and missing information: The abstract ends with an incomplete placeholder ('Our code is available at .'), and there are numerous typos throughout the paper (e.g., 'Clien-wise Non-IID' in Figure 1, 'Lipschitz Dmooth' in Assumption D.4, 'gradient obays' in Assumption D.2, and 'L = 1'' in Algorithm 2).

strengths: Intuitive and well-motivated framework: real-world federated learning settings often contain hierarchical or multi-granular non-IID data distributions (spanning globally shared patterns, subgroup/cluster patterns, and client-specific patterns).

Pragmatic system design: the progressive, stage-wise additive training scheme (optimizing one level at a time while keeping earlier levels frozen) avoids the instability of simultaneously training multiple interacting models and keeps per-round communication cost equivalent to single-model FL.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is evaluated across three distinct non-IID partition schemes (cluster-wise, Dirichlet client-wise, and hierarchical multi-level) on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet, supported by insightful visualizations of the learned cluster structures.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison regarding model capacity and ensembling: In FeMAM, each client maintains and executes an additive ensemble of up to $L=5$ ResNet-9 models. In contrast, all evaluated baselines (FedAvg, Ditto, pFedMe, FeSEM, etc.) utilize only a single ResNet-9 model. Standard deep learning ensembles are well known to provide significant performance boosts; it is unclear whether the observed empirical gains stem from the multi-level structure or simply from an ensemble of 5 ResNet-9 models. The paper lacks parameter-matched baselines (e.g., a single wider/deeper model matching total FLOPs/parameters) or federated ensembling/boosting baselines.

Fundamental flaws in the convergence analysis: In Theorem 2 / Theorem D.2, the learning rate upper bound is given as $\eta \le \min \{ \dots,  rac{\|
abla\|^2 - B U^2}{\|
abla\|^2 + \sigma^2}  rac{2}{ eta} \}$. When the gradient norm is small ($\|
abla\|^2 < B U^2$, which inevitably occurs near stationary points), the right-hand side becomes strictly negative. Since the learning rate $\eta$ must be strictly positive, this condition cannot hold, invalidating the claim of monotonic descent and convergence to an $\epsilon$-stationary point. Furthermore, the step-size condition in Theorem 1 depends on $\|	heta_i^{(t)} - \Theta_{C_l(i)}^{(l)}\|$, which vanishes as models converge to cluster centroids, implying the step size must shrink to zero.

Disconnect between theoretical proof and practical algorithm: The convergence proof in Appendix D.4 explicitly analyzes the simultaneous update of all $L$ levels at every local step $q$ (e.g., page 22 telescoping over all levels simultaneously). However, Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 operate via stage-wise greedy training, where earlier levels $1, \dots, L'-1$ are strictly frozen while only level $L'$ is trained. The theoretical model thus does not reflect the algorithm actually deployed and evaluated.

Limited conceptual novelty over prior clustered additive FL: Clustered additive modeling combining global, cluster, and personalized models was already introduced by Ma et al. (NeurIPS 2023, ref [34]). FeMAM essentially generalizes this from 3 fixed levels to $L$ levels trained sequentially, which represents an incremental extension.

Presentation and mathematical drafting issues: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and grammatical errors in formal sections, such as 'Lipshitz Dmooth' (Assumption D.4), 'Covergence' (Theorem D.2), 'obays' (Assumption D.2), 'Clien-wise Non-IID' (Figure 1 caption), and 'expect that we rotated' (Section C.3).

strengths: The conceptual motivation of addressing hierarchical or multi-granularity non-IID structures in federated learning is well-articulated and relevant to real-world deployment scenarios.

The empirical evaluation covers multiple datasets (CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet) across diverse non-IID partitioning strategies, showing solid predictive improvements over standard clustered and personalized federated baselines.

The model pruning mechanism (Eq. 9) provides an intuitive, adaptive criterion allowing clients to reject levels that do not improve local validation error, providing variable model complexity across clients.
weaknesses: Theoretical soundness issues in the convergence analysis: Theorem 2 requires the learning rate $\eta$ to satisfy $\eta \le \frac{\|g\|^2 - BU^2}{\|g\|^2 + \sigma^2} \cdot \frac{2}{\beta}$. When the local gradient norm satisfies $\|g\|^2 < BU^2$, the upper bound becomes strictly negative, making the required learning rate non-positive and the theorem vacuous near stationary points. Furthermore, the proof in Appendix D treats the objective as convex directly with respect to the neural network parameters $\theta$ (e.g., page 21, asserting $\ell(\dots, \Theta) - \ell(\dots, \theta) \le \langle \nabla_\Theta \ell, \Theta - \theta \rangle$), which does not hold for deep neural networks such as the ResNet-9 architecture used in the experiments.

Unfair capacity and missing ensemble baselines: FeMAM constructs an additive ensemble of up to $L=5$ full ResNet-9 models per client. The manuscript compares FeMAM against baselines (FedAvg, Ditto, PFedMe, FeSEM) that train only a single ResNet-9 model. It is unclear how much of the performance advantage stems from the multi-level structure versus simply having up to $5\times$ the parameter capacity, memory footprint, and inference FLOPs. Parameter-matched baselines or standard ensemble federated baselines are essential to isolate the source of improvement.

Incremental algorithmic novelty: The formulation strongly resembles existing federated additive modeling works (e.g., Ma et al., NeurIPS 2023; Li et al., 2023), extending two-level additive modeling (global + cluster or global + local) to a greedy, multi-stage pipeline with K-means clustering.

High cumulative latency and sequential training overhead: FeMAM trains levels strictly sequentially, waiting for convergence at level $l$ before training level $l+1$. The first level alone takes 400 rounds, followed by multiple rounds per subsequent level (reaching 600–700 total communication rounds), which substantially limits practical applicability in communication-constrained environments.

Presentation and writing polish: Several typographical and formal errors are present throughout the text and appendix (e.g., 'Clien-wise' in Figure 1, 'Lipschitz Dmooth' in Assumption D.4, 'obays' in Assumption D.2, and an empty code repository placeholder in the abstract: 'Our code is available at .').

strengths: Well-motivated formulation: The paper effectively articulates the need for multi-level federated learning that captures coarse-to-fine sharing (global, subgroup/cluster, and local/personalized) without imposing rigid, predefined cluster hierarchies.

Efficient and adaptive boosting-like design: By training level-by-level and freezing earlier levels, FeMAM maintains per-round communication and computation costs identical to single-model FL during training. The client-side structure pruning naturally tailors personalization depth to individual client heterogeneity.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The authors evaluate FeMAM against strong baselines across multiple challenging settings, including synthetic multi-level partitions, standard Dirichlet client-wise partitions, and a modern LLM PEFT setup (Qwen3-4B with LoRA across 71 distinct FLAN-T5 tasks). FeMAM consistently demonstrates strong gains across both accuracy/ROUGE and convergence stability.

Informative empirical analysis: Visualizations of client-level model count distributions (Figures 5, 8, and A.1) provide clear evidence that clients automatically prune levels according to the complexity of the underlying data distribution (e.g., retaining 1 level under IID vs. multiple levels under heavy non-IID).
weaknesses: Discrepancy between theoretical boosting step size and practical implementation: In the convergence proof (Section D.5, Equations D.15–D.17), the strict descent rate assumes an optimal step size/shrinkage factor \(\eta = \frac{\langle g^{(<l)}, h^{(l)} \rangle}{\beta \|h^{(l)}\|^2}\) is multiplied with the new level. In the algorithmic implementation (Equations 2, 6, and Algorithm 1), levels are simply summed unweighted (unit step size). While validation-based pruning guarantees empirical non-increase, the theory relies on this step-size assumption which should be clarified in the main text.

Inference overhead for full-parameter models: While training communication is preserved at 1 model per round, at test time a client must evaluate up to \(L\) models. For LoRA adapters (as in the LLM experiment), this is trivial via adapter merging/weight addition, but for full-parameter vision backbones (ResNet-9), storing and forward-passing multiple independent models linearly scales client-side memory footprint and inference compute.

Ablation on level ordering and routing criteria: FeMAM assumes a fixed coarse-to-fine sequence (Global FedAvg \(\to\) Clustered FL \(\to\) Local personalization). The paper does not thoroughly discuss or evaluate whether the ordering matters, nor how alternative level routing criteria (e.g., loss-based IFCA routing vs. distance-to-centroid K-means) affect intermediate cluster stability.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated framework: Extending federated learning beyond flat clustering and simple global-plus-local dichotomies to multi-level, coarse-to-fine structures addresses a genuine limitation of existing personalized FL algorithms.

Efficient sequential optimization paradigm: The boosting-style level-wise training—optimizing and communicating only one level per round while freezing previously converged levels—elegantly maintains the per-round communication and local training compute overhead comparable to single-model FL.

Adaptive structure pruning: The validation-based pruning mechanism provides an automatic way to prevent overfitting and avoid unnecessary model depth, enabling clients with varying data complexities or computational capacities to adaptively retain only utility-improving levels.

Thorough empirical evaluation: Experiments include diverse non-IID benchmarks (Cluster-wise, Client-wise Dirichlet, and Multi-level) on standard vision datasets (CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) as well as contemporary PEFT instruction-tuning on Qwen3-4B with 71 Flan-T5 tasks, consistently demonstrating strong performance against representative baselines.
Clear presentation: The paper is well structured, with clear architectural diagrams, informative convergence trajectories, and transparent ablation studies regarding depth L and cluster count K.
weaknesses: Inference memory and compute overhead: In the standard vision instantiation, FeMAM uses independent ResNet-9 models across levels, requiring clients to store and execute forward passes through up to L models at test time. While per-round training communication is lightweight, an L-fold increase in parameter footprint and FLOPs at inference compared to single-model baselines is non-negligible, and the paper does not thoroughly discuss baseline comparisons scaled to equivalent parameter/compute budgets.

Gap between boosting theory and empirical implementation: The theoretical convergence across levels in Section 4.3 and Appendix D.5 assumes an optimal step size/shrinkage on the level outputs and posits Assumption D.5 (residual alignment / boosting edge). In practice, models are simply summed unweighted (equivalent to fixed step size = 1) and Assumption D.5 is assumed rather than guaranteed by the local SGD dynamics.

Discrepancy between training objective and validation pruning: Lemma D.14 assumes monotonic reduction in the training loss via pruning, whereas Algorithm 1 and Equation (7) prune models based on validation error. Pruning on validation data does not theoretically ensure non-increasing training loss R_l.

Fixed heuristic communication schedule: The level-wise schedule allocates a fixed 400 rounds to Level 1 and 50 rounds to subsequent levels in the vision benchmark. It remains unclear how sensitive the final model quality is to this allocation, or how well this heuristic transfers to settings with varying client speeds, data sizes, or non-IID severities.

strengths: Relevant and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper targets multi-level non-IID heterogeneity in federated learning, capturing hierarchical relationships (global, subgroup, and client-specific) which are common in real-world applications but often oversimplified by standard global, clustered, or two-level personalized FL methods.

Practical and communication-efficient design: The level-wise boosting-style training procedure updates and communicates only one level at a time while freezing lower levels. This maintains the per-round communication footprint of single-model FL while constructing an additive hierarchy.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors validate the method across multiple benchmark datasets (CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet) under various non-IID partitions (cluster-wise, Dirichlet client-wise, and explicit multi-level), as well as a large-scale setting using Qwen3-4B LoRA fine-tuning on FLAN-T5 tasks.

Insightful ablation and structural analysis: The paper includes informative analyses of client-specific depth distributions (Figures 5 and 8), showing that clients adaptively retain different numbers of models depending on the underlying data heterogeneity, supported by sensitivity studies over L and K.
weaknesses: Disconnect between theoretical analysis and algorithmic implementation: The convergence analysis in Section 4.3 and Appendix D relies on standard functional gradient boosting descent (Eq. D.15–D.16), which requires choosing an optimal shrinkage/step-size \(\eta^* = \frac{\langle g, h \rangle}{\beta \|h\|^2}\). However, the actual algorithm (Eq. 2, Eq. 6, and Algorithm 1) does not use a learned or line-searched shrinkage parameter across levels, but instead directly adds unscaled model predictions (\(\eta = 1\)). Moreover, the theory bounds training loss under parameter SGD, whereas structure pruning is performed on local validation loss (Eq. 7), breaking the formal guarantee of monotonic descent in Eq. (D.17).

Unfair model capacity and inference budget comparison: At inference time, clients running FeMAM retain on average 4.7 models for client-wise and multi-level settings (Table 4), effectively evaluating an ensemble of up to 5 full ResNet-9 networks or LoRA adapters. In contrast, standard baselines (FedAvg, Ditto, FedAvg+) utilize only 1 or 2 models. It is unclear how much of the performance gain is due to the multi-level structure versus simply evaluating a significantly larger parameter ensemble.

Heuristic specification of intermediate levels: In the instantiated setup (Table 2), Levels 2, 3, and 4 all use identical K-means clustering with the same number of clusters (\(K_l = 5\)). The paper provides little theoretical or algorithmic justification for why stacking multiple identical cluster sizes discovers distinct granularities rather than redundant representations, relying almost entirely on client-side validation pruning to discard unhelpful levels post-hoc.

Tightly bounded assumptions without proof: Key theoretical assumptions are overly strong and essentially assume the desired result; for example, Assumption D.4 simply assumes by definition that cluster assignment introduces bounded slack \(\varepsilon_l\), and Assumption D.5 posits a boosting alignment edge \(\gamma_l > 0\) without analyzing whether federated SGD across non-IID clients can guarantee positive correlation with functional residuals in non-convex neural network settings.

Modest gains in foundation model benchmark: In Table 5 (Qwen3-4B LoRA on FLAN-T5 tasks), FeMAM achieves a ROUGE-1 score of 59.25%, which is only a marginal improvement over existing clustered baselines like FeSEM (58.65%) and FedCAM (58.00%), despite requiring clients to store and evaluate up to 4 distinct LoRA adapters.
